nameStory: The lazuli bunting gets its stunning name from lapis lazuli, the brilliant blue gemstone prized since ancient times. When early naturalists saw the male's vibrant turquoise-blue head and wings, they immediately thought of this precious stone. It's a name that perfectly captures the bird's jewel-like beauty.
description: The lazuli bunting is a small, sparrow-sized songbird that brings a flash of brilliant blue to western landscapes. Males are showstoppers with their bright turquoise-blue heads, backs, and wings, contrasted by a rusty-orange breast band and white belly. Females are much more subdued, wearing soft brown and gray tones with subtle blue hints on their wings and tail. These compact birds measure about 5-6 inches long, making them smaller than a robin but larger than a chickadee.

idTips.label: Male's blue coloring
idTips.description: Brilliant turquoise-blue head, back, and wings that shimmer almost metallic in sunlight, unlike any other small bird in the region

idTips.label: Orange breast band
idTips.description: Males sport a distinctive rusty-orange band across the chest, creating a striking contrast with the blue above and white below

idTips.label: Female's subtle blue
idTips.description: Females show just hints of blue on wings and tail, appearing mostly warm brown overall with a lighter, buffy breast

idTips.label: Thick seed-cracking bill
idTips.description: Short, thick, cone-shaped bill perfect for cracking seeds, darker on top and lighter below

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Compact and stocky like other buntings, with a relatively large head and short tail that gives them a chunky appearance

habitat: In New England, lazuli buntings are extremely rare visitors, with only 11 recorded sightings. When they do appear, it's typically during migration in areas with scattered trees and shrubland, such as forest edges, overgrown fields, or brushy areas near water. They prefer semi-open habitats rather than dense forests or completely open grasslands.

seasonality.spring: Your best chance to spot this rarity during spring migration, typically May through early June. Listen for their sweet, varied songs from prominent perches.
seasonality.summer: Virtually absent from New England during breeding season, as they nest in western North America. Any summer sighting would be exceptional.
seasonality.fall: Possible but extremely rare during fall migration, usually August through September. Males may show duller colors, making identification more challenging.
seasonality.winter: Not present in New England during winter months, as they migrate to Mexico and Central America.

funFact: Lazuli buntings are musical copycats - young males learn their songs not just from their fathers, but by eavesdropping on neighboring males, creating local 'song dialects' where birds in the same area share similar tunes, like regional accents in the bird world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the more common Indigo Bunting, but male lazulis have that distinctive orange breast band and turquoise (rather than deep blue) coloring. Remember: 'Lazuli has the orange belly band, Indigo is all blue.' Female lazulis are browner overall compared to the grayer female Indigo Buntings.
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily a western species, so any New England sighting is noteworthy and should be reported to eBird. The extreme rarity means many birders go their entire lives without seeing one in our region, making it a true prize for anyone lucky enough to encounter this western wanderer.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Indigo Bunting, lazulis are lighter blue (turquoise vs. deep blue) and males have that telltale orange breast band that Indigos lack entirely. Unlike the massive Blue Grosbeak with its thick bill and rusty wing bars, lazuli buntings are smaller with finer features. The tropical Painted Bunting, while in the same genus, looks completely different with its rainbow of colors including red and green.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While Indigo Buntings are the only member of their bunting genus commonly seen in New England, they're related to Blue Grosbeaks which are larger with rusty wing bars and rarely venture this far north.
Among its bunting relatives, the Blue Grosbeak is much larger and more robust than the Indigo Bunting, with that signature thick bill and rusty wing bars that Indigo Buntings lack entirely.
Painted Buntings are much more colorful than their close relative, the Indigo Bunting - males are rainbow-colored versus solid blue, and females are bright yellow-green versus brown.
